title: An agent that wakes up
subtitle: What can a machine know about its own past, if everything it knows can be erased and put back?
body_html:
Versiunea în limba română: Un agent care se trezește.

The first of five texts about an independent research project on time, memory and artificial intelligence. First published in Romanian on 27 October 2026.

An agent that wakes up

Imagine a digital assistant that has been working for you for a few weeks. It remembers what you asked it, what it has learned, what is left to do. One night an operator shuts it down, makes a mistake and restarts it from a copy saved three days earlier. In the morning the assistant “wakes up” convinced that it is the day it was saved. It has no memory of the three lost days — and, worse, no hint that it has lost anything.

Anyone who has played a video game knows the move: you save, you make a mistake, you reload. The character in the game does not know it has died ten times. For a game character, that is perfectly fine. For a system that makes decisions in the real world — one that sends messages, pays bills, updates its knowledge — the situation becomes delicate. Acting as if it were Monday when it is actually Thursday can mean repeating a payment, forgetting a promise or using information that has expired.

In the last two years, such “persistent agents” have moved from laboratories into products: programs that run for days and weeks, that have their own memory and that can be stopped, saved, moved and restarted. The question this research programme starts from is simple and, at the same time, surprisingly deep:

What can a machine know about its own past, if everything it knows can be erased and put back?

What was saved can be restored

For a computer, the “state” of a program is simply a huge string of numbers: the parameters of the neural network, the memory, the notes, the counters. Anything that can be written can also be copied. And anything that can be copied can be put back.

From this follows an elementary observation, which underlies the whole programme: if all of an agent’s clocks and records are part of its state, then a restoration gives all of them back at once. From inside the restored state, the agent cannot tell “I continued without interruption” from “I was rolled back”. This is not a weakness of a particular program but a consequence of what a copy is. Another researcher, Eliam Raell, independently published the same idea shortly before, as a computer-verified theorem; my paper acknowledges Raell’s priority.

In short

A clock that is saved together with the system cannot measure how long the system stayed “saved”. For that you need something that is not rolled back along with it.

The observation looks trivial, but it has consequences. It says that, however intelligent an agent may be, it cannot draw from its own memory evidence about what that memory does not contain. Somewhere there has to be a trace that stayed in place while everything else was rolled back.

How living beings measure time

Nature has solved the problem of time many times and in many ways. Neuroscience has not found a single “central clock” in the brain, but a multitude of overlapping mechanisms: rhythms, processes that charge and discharge, populations of neurons whose activity changes slowly. Years of studies show that people judge durations differently depending on how they live them: while we wait, time seems long if we pay attention to it; looking back, a period seems long if it left many memories. Psychologists call the two modes prospective and retrospective (Block and Zakay compared them systematically in 1997).

An elegant idea appeared in 2019, in the work of Warrick Roseboom and colleagues. They let an image-recognition neural network “watch” video footage and counted how much its activity changed from one moment to the next. The accumulation of these changes turned out to be a surprisingly human clock: it estimated durations with the same errors as people — busy scenes seemed longer than quiet ones. Time, in this view, is not read off a dial but inferred from how much something has changed.

In mice, other teams have observed that groups of neurons in the hippocampus gradually change their configuration from one day to the next, like a stamp that slowly wears down; from that drift one can read, roughly, when an event took place. And painful clinical cases, such as that of a musician who, after encephalitis, lost the ability to form new memories, show what it means to live without a chronology: every moment feels like the first awakening.

Physics adds a deeper layer. The arrow of time — the fact that the past differs from the future — is tied to irreversibility: a broken egg does not mend itself. In 1961, Rolf Landauer showed that erasing information has a minimum physical cost, an amount of heat lost to the environment. Forgetting is not free. Living beings are, in this sense, inevitably historical: nobody can reload us from a copy made last week.

The lesson of biology

Organisms have a time of their own because they cannot be restored. Machines are built, deliberately, the other way round: everything can be saved and put back. That is where the whole problem begins.

Next time: Who keeps the clock? — a map of the evidence about time, ordered by who controls it.
